issues.issue: The carve-out "except with respect to an injury or other loss which occurs on lands whose rules or regulations prohibit my doing so as a matter of law" makes the scope of the assumption depend on unidentified land-manager rules, and "my doing so" has no clear antecedent. Whether a given permit or agency regulation triggers the exception is left entirely open.

The release reaches claims "arising in whole or part from my, or the minor student's, enrollment or participation in an activity of NOLS," and neither "an activity of NOLS" nor the "in whole or part" causal link is defined. Whether an injury occurring outside supervised programming falls inside that phrase is precisely the sort of question parties litigate.

The release of "any and all claims" against staff must be squared with the Free Time bullet, which says staff assisting students in free time act "as private individuals" and that NOLS is not responsible for their conduct. The two provisions define the protected conduct of the same people differently.

The indemnity runs against claims by "a member of my ... family, a rescuer, another student, or any other person," a general catch-all appended to specific categories whose reach is uncertain under ejusdem generis. It also covers losses "suffered by me or caused by me," which on its face would require the promisor to indemnify NOLS against the promisor's own claim.

The carve-outs turn on the undefined boundary between "negligence" and "gross negligence or intentionally wrongful conduct," and on "lands whose rules or regulations prohibit such agreements as a matter of law." The added instruction that the release be "enforced to the fullest extent permitted by law" tells a court to determine the clause's scope rather than fixing it.

This paragraph limits the release to ordinary negligence, while the Acknowledgment and Assumption paragraph has the signer "expressly assume ALL risks ... inherent or otherwise, and whether or not described above" without any gross-negligence carve-out. Which limitation governs a gross-negligence claim is a genuine internal tension.

The health warranty is qualified by "or otherwise satisfied NOLS" and by conditions "that might affect" participation, standards with no ascertainable boundary. NOLS's reserved right to remove a student "for any reason it deems in the best interests of the student or the school" is likewise unbounded discretion.

"Costs reasonably associated with medical services, including evacuation" leaves the reasonableness limit and the range of chargeable services undefined. Whether a costly rescue or evacuation falls inside the phrase is arguable.

The undertaking to be responsible for "any damage" to NOLS facilities or gear is unqualified by fault, so it may be read as strict liability or as limited to negligent damage. That reading is not resolved anywhere in the document.

"Shall occur or be filed only in the State of Wyoming" is ambiguous between a geographic requirement (any court sitting in Wyoming, including the federal district court) and a requirement of Wyoming state courts. "Any mediation or suit" also leaves unclear whether mediation is required at all or merely venued if it occurs.

The forum restriction sits with the choice-of-law sentence in the same paragraph selecting Wyoming substantive law, and must be reconciled with the severability clause if the forum term is held unenforceable in the chosen forum. No direct contradiction with another operative term appears.

Severability would be invoked if the release or the parent's undertaking on behalf of the minor were held invalid, and the document contains no statement of which terms are essential; the binding-effect block instead states the whole agreement binds student, parent, heirs and estate. How much of the release survives partial invalidity is left to construction.

The block purports to bind "THE STUDENT AND THE PARENT(S) OR GUARDIAN OF A MINOR STUDENT" and their heirs and estates, but the signature block provides only a student signature line and a separate, conditional parent line. Whether the terms bind a minor student, or heirs who never signed, turns on this wording.

The recital that the signers "HAVE READ THIS PAGE AND THE PREVIOUS 3 PAGES" must be squared with the header, which requires a parent signature for minors as evidence of the parent's agreement, and with the parent line left for signature only "if the student or participant is a minor." The document therefore asserts assent by persons whose signature it makes optional.

The written-modification requirement must be read with the incorporation of the Catalog, website, Admission Policies and "other material provided by NOLS," which allows outside documents to bear on the parties' obligations without any integration clause. That leaves the scope of "the Agreement" that can only be modified in writing uncertain.
